claim: The Turing reaction-diffusion model explains how identical cells can self-organize to form spatial patterns.
source: The Turing reaction-diffusion model explains how identical cells can self-organize to form spatial patterns.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about the Turing model, supported by established scientific knowledge and the citation to Turing's original work.

claim: It has been suggested that extracellular signaling molecules with different diffusion coefficients underlie the Turing model.
source: It has been suggested that extracellular signaling molecules with different diffusion coefficients underlie this model, but the contribution of cell-autonomous signaling components is largely unknown.
evidence: This claim references previous suggestions in the literature about differential diffusion requirements.

claim: The contribution of cell-autonomous signaling components to Turing patterning is largely unknown.
source: It has been suggested that extracellular signaling molecules with different diffusion coefficients underlie this model, but the contribution of cell-autonomous signaling components is largely unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge about cell-autonomous factors in reaction-diffusion systems.

claim: In the presence of cell-autonomous factors, networks can form a pattern with equally diffusing signals.
source: This analysis reveals that in the presence of cell-autonomous factors, networks can form a pattern with equally diffusing signals and even for any combination of diffusion coefficients.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the automated mathematical analysis performed in the study.

claim: Networks can form patterns for any combination of diffusion coefficients when cell-autonomous factors are present.
source: This analysis reveals that in the presence of cell-autonomous factors, networks can form a pattern with equally diffusing signals and even for any combination of diffusion coefficients.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mathematical analysis, specifically referring to Type III networks.

claim: The software RDNets is available at http://www.RDNets.com.
source: We provide a software (available at http://www.RDNets.com) to explore these networks and to constrain topologies with qualitative and quantitative experimental data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of the software.

claim: RDNets can constrain network topologies with qualitative and quantitative experimental data.
source: We provide a software (available at http://www.RDNets.com) to explore these networks and to constrain topologies with qualitative and quantitative experimental data.
evidence: This describes a capability of the software demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The software was used to examine self-organizing networks that control embryonic axis specification.
source: We use the software to examine the self-organizing networks that control embryonic axis specification and digit patterning.
evidence: This describes an application of the software to a specific developmental system.

claim: The software was used to examine self-organizing networks that control digit patterning.
source: We use the software to examine the self-organizing networks that control embryonic axis specification and digit patterning.
evidence: This describes an application of the software to a specific developmental system.

claim: Existing synthetic circuits can be extended with additional feedbacks to form Turing reaction-diffusion systems.
source: Finally, we demonstrate how existing synthetic circuits can be extended with additional feedbacks to form Turing reaction-diffusion systems.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the analysis of the Chen and Weiss synthetic circuit.

claim: Alan Turing proposed a theoretical model in which interactions between diffusible substances can break the initial symmetry of cell fields to form periodic patterns more than six decades ago.
source: More than six decades ago, Alan Turing proposed a theoretical model in which interactions between diffusible substances can break the initial symmetry of cell fields to form periodic patterns (Turing, 1952).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Turing's original 1952 paper.

claim: Gierer and Meinhardt postulated that self-organizing processes require differential diffusivity between a short-range self-enhancing activator and a feedback-induced long-range inhibitor.
source: Subsequent work from Gierer and Meinhardt postulated that such self-organizing processes require differential diffusivity between a short-range self-enhancing activator and a feedback-induced long-range inhibitor (Gierer and Meinhardt, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Gierer and Meinhardt 1972 paper.

claim: Numerous studies have proposed models based on activator-inhibitor concepts to explain pattern formation during development.
source: Numerous studies have proposed models based on these concepts to explain pattern formation during development, including skin appendage specification (Sick et al., 2006; Harris et al., 2005), lung branching (Menshykau et al., 2012; Hagiwara et al., 2015), tooth development (Salazar-Ciudad and Jernvall, 2010), rugae formation (Economou et al., 2012), and digit patterning (Sheth et al., 2012; Raspopovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in different developmental contexts.

claim: Evidence in support of specific activator-inhibitor pairs has been limited.
source: However, the evidence in support of specific activator-inhibitor pairs has been limited, and few studies have provided experimental support for the differential diffusivity of activators and inhibitors (Kondo and Miura, 2010; Marcon and Sharpe, 2012; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: Few studies have provided experimental support for the differential diffusivity of activators and inhibitors.
source: However, the evidence in support of specific activator-inhibitor pairs has been limited, and few studies have provided experimental support for the differential diffusivity of activators and inhibitors (Kondo and Miura, 2010; Marcon and Sharpe, 2012; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: Most reaction-diffusion models have been reduced to abstract networks of two diffusible reactants.
source: However, since most reaction-diffusion models have been reduced to abstract networks of two diffusible reactants, the influence of immobile cell-autonomous factors on reaction-diffusion patterning is largely unknown.
evidence: This describes the current state of modeling approaches in the field.

claim: Previous theoretical studies on selected network topologies have challenged the differential diffusivity requirements.
source: Previous theoretical studies on selected network topologies have challenged the differential diffusivity requirements and indicated that in the presence of an immobile substance, patterns can form for a wider range of reaction and diffusion parameters (Othmer and Scriven, 1969; Pearson and Horsthemke, 1989; Pearson, 1992; Pearson and Bruno, 1992; Rauch and Millonas, 2004; Levine and Rappel, 2005; Miura et al., 2009; Raspopovic et al., 2014; Korvasova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: In the presence of an immobile substance, patterns can form for a wider range of reaction and diffusion parameters.
source: Previous theoretical studies on selected network topologies have challenged the differential diffusivity requirements and indicated that in the presence of an immobile substance, patterns can form for a wider range of reaction and diffusion parameters (Othmer and Scriven, 1969; Pearson and Horsthemke, 1989; Pearson, 1992; Pearson and Bruno, 1992; Rauch and Millonas, 2004; Levine and Rappel, 2005; Miura et al., 2009; Raspopovic et al., 2014; Korvasova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Extending models beyond abstract two-node systems can reveal different pattern formation requirements.
source: These and other studies (Meinhardt, 2004; Werner et al., 2015) suggest that extending models beyond abstract two-node systems can reveal different pattern formation requirements and may uncover new biologically relevant network designs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous studies cited in the text.

claim: Extending models beyond abstract two-node systems may uncover new biologically relevant network designs.
source: These and other studies (Meinhardt, 2004; Werner et al., 2015) suggest that extending models beyond abstract two-node systems can reveal different pattern formation requirements and may uncover new biologically relevant network designs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous studies cited in the text.

claim: Extending reaction-diffusion models to more realistic signaling networks has been challenging due to complex mathematical analysis required.
source: However, due to the complex mathematical analysis required to identify and understand such systems, extending reaction-diffusion models to more realistic signaling networks has been challenging, and the main assumption in the field has remained that complex models should reduce to simple systems that require an effective differential diffusivity.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the field based on the complexity of mathematical analysis.

claim: The main assumption in the field has remained that complex models should reduce to simple systems that require an effective differential diffusivity.
source: However, due to the complex mathematical analysis required to identify and understand such systems, extending reaction-diffusion models to more realistic signaling networks has been challenging, and the main assumption in the field has remained that complex models should reduce to simple systems that require an effective differential diffusivity.
evidence: This describes the prevailing assumption in the field.

claim: RDNets performs a high-throughput mathematical analysis of complex reaction-diffusion networks with non-diffusible components.
source: Here, we developed the freely available and user-friendly software RDNets (available at http://www.RDNets.com) to perform a high-throughput mathematical analysis of complex reaction-diffusion networks with non-diffusible components.
evidence: This describes the functionality of the software developed in the study.

claim: RDNets guarantees completeness, reproducibility, and detailed mechanistic insights compared to previous numerical studies.
source: In comparison to previous numerical studies, this method guarantees completeness, reproducibility, and detailed mechanistic insights into the principles underlying pattern formation.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the analytical approach used in RDNets.

claim: RDNets was used to build a comprehensive catalog of minimal three-node and four-node reaction-diffusion networks.
source: We used RDNets to build a comprehensive catalog of minimal three-node and four-node reaction-diffusion networks that include interactions between diffusible signals and cell-autonomous factors.
evidence: This describes the application of the software to generate a catalog of networks.

claim: Reaction-diffusion systems have three types of requirements for the diffusible signals depending on the network topology.
source: Our results show that reaction-diffusion systems have three types of requirements for the diffusible signals depending on the network topology: Type I networks require differential diffusivity, Type II networks allow equal diffusivities, and Type III networks allow for unconstrained diffusivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Type I networks require differential diffusivity.
source: Our results show that reaction-diffusion systems have three types of requirements for the diffusible signals depending on the network topology: Type I networks require differential diffusivity, Type II networks allow equal diffusivities, and Type III networks allow for unconstrained diffusivity.
evidence: This is a classification result from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Type II networks allow equal diffusivities.
source: Our results show that reaction-diffusion systems have three types of requirements for the diffusible signals depending on the network topology: Type I networks require differential diffusivity, Type II networks allow equal diffusivities, and Type III networks allow for unconstrained diffusivity.
evidence: This is a classification result from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Type III networks allow for unconstrained diffusivity.
source: Our results show that reaction-diffusion systems have three types of requirements for the diffusible signals depending on the network topology: Type I networks require differential diffusivity, Type II networks allow equal diffusivities, and Type III networks allow for unconstrained diffusivity.
evidence: This is a classification result from the mathematical analysis.

claim: 70% of the networks identified by the analysis are of Type II and Type III.
source: Overall, 70% of the networks identified by our analysis are of Type II and Type III and thus do not require differential diffusivity to form a spatial pattern.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the catalog of networks generated.

claim: 70% of identified networks do not require differential diffusivity to form a spatial pattern.
source: Overall, 70% of the networks identified by our analysis are of Type II and Type III and thus do not require differential diffusivity to form a spatial pattern.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the catalog of networks generated.

claim: Realistic reaction-diffusion systems are based on mechanisms that are fundamentally different from the concepts of short-range activation and long-range inhibition based on differential diffusivity.
source: This reveals that realistic reaction-diffusion systems are based on mechanisms that are fundamentally different from the concepts of short-range activation and long-range inhibition based on differential diffusivity (Gierer and Meinhardt, 1972) that have been predominant in previous models of pattern formation.
evidence: This is a major conclusion drawn from the finding that 70% of networks don't require differential diffusivity.

claim: Understanding how complex gene regulatory networks control cellular behavior is a challenging problem in biology.
source: Understanding how complex gene regulatory networks control cellular behavior is a challenging problem in biology; even small networks can contain regulatory feedbacks that make systems behaviors difficult to predict (Le Novère, 2015).
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by citation.

claim: Even small networks can contain regulatory feedbacks that make systems behaviors difficult to predict.
source: Understanding how complex gene regulatory networks control cellular behavior is a challenging problem in biology; even small networks can contain regulatory feedbacks that make systems behaviors difficult to predict (Le Novère, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation and describes a known challenge in systems biology.

claim: Mathematical biology has helped to identify network motifs that underlie basic behaviors such as oscillations, bi-stability or noise reduction.
source: Mathematical biology has helped to identify network motifs that underlie basic behaviors such as oscillations, bi-stability or noise reduction (Kepler and Elston, 2001; Shen-Orr et al., 2002; Mangan and Alon, 2003), but this approach has been difficult to scale up to more complex networks and behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in mathematical biology.

claim: Mathematical biology approaches have been difficult to scale up to more complex networks and behaviors.
source: Mathematical biology has helped to identify network motifs that underlie basic behaviors such as oscillations, bi-stability or noise reduction (Kepler and Elston, 2001; Shen-Orr et al., 2002; Mangan and Alon, 2003), but this approach has been difficult to scale up to more complex networks and behaviors.
evidence: This describes a limitation of previous mathematical approaches.

claim: Previous studies have overcome the scaling obstacle by using numerical simulations to screen for topologies that implement a certain behavior.
source: Previous studies have overcome this obstacle by using numerical simulations to screen for topologies that implement a certain behavior (Salazar-Ciudad et al., 2000; Ma et al., 2009; Cotterell and Sharpe, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous numerical screening studies.

claim: Numerical simulations demand large computational power.
source: However, such simulations demand large computational power, their coverage is incomplete, and they do not have the explanatory power of analytical approaches.
evidence: This describes a limitation of numerical simulation approaches.

claim: Numerical simulations have incomplete coverage.
source: However, such simulations demand large computational power, their coverage is incomplete, and they do not have the explanatory power of analytical approaches.
evidence: This describes a limitation of numerical simulation approaches.

claim: Numerical simulations do not have the explanatory power of analytical approaches.
source: However, such simulations demand large computational power, their coverage is incomplete, and they do not have the explanatory power of analytical approaches.
evidence: This describes a limitation of numerical simulation approaches compared to analytical methods.

claim: RDNets uses automated linear stability analysis to derive pattern forming conditions of networks with N nodes.
source: We developed an automated linear stability analysis (Murray, 2003) to derive the pattern forming conditions of networks with N nodes (Figure 1a, Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the software, with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Linear stability analysis determines whether a system can form a pattern by testing if the concentrations of the reactants are stable at steady state.
source: Linear stability analysis determines whether a system can form a pattern by testing i) if the concentrations of the reactants are stable at steady state, and ii) if diffusion-driven instabilities arise with small perturbations.
evidence: This describes the principle of linear stability analysis.

claim: Linear stability analysis determines whether a system can form a pattern by testing if diffusion-driven instabilities arise with small perturbations.
source: Linear stability analysis determines whether a system can form a pattern by testing i) if the concentrations of the reactants are stable at steady state, and ii) if diffusion-driven instabilities arise with small perturbations.
evidence: This describes the principle of linear stability analysis.

claim: Linear stability analysis has been the exclusive domain of mathematicians and systems biologists due to its mathematical complexity.
source: Because of its mathematical complexity, this type of analysis has been the exclusive domain of mathematicians and systems biologists (Koch and Meinhardt, 1994; Satnoianu et al., 2000; Murray, 2003; Miura and Maini, 2004), and its application beyond two-reactant models has required dedicated theoretical studies for selected networks (Othmer and Scriven, 1971; White and Gilligan, 1998; Klika et al., 2012; Korvasova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations and describes the historical limitation of the approach.

claim: Application of linear stability analysis beyond two-reactant models has required dedicated theoretical studies for selected networks.
source: Because of its mathematical complexity, this type of analysis has been the exclusive domain of mathematicians and systems biologists (Koch and Meinhardt, 1994; Satnoianu et al., 2000; Murray, 2003; Miura and Maini, 2004), and its application beyond two-reactant models has required dedicated theoretical studies for selected networks (Othmer and Scriven, 1971; White and Gilligan, 1998; Klika et al., 2012; Korvasova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical studies.

claim: RDNets utilized a modern computer algebra system to automate the algebraic calculations.
source: To generalize the analysis to networks with more than two nodes, we utilized a modern computer algebra system and developed the software pipeline RDNets that automates the algebraic calculations.
evidence: This describes the technical approach used to develop the software.

claim: Secreted molecules like ligands and extracellular inhibitors are represented by diffusible nodes in RDNets.
source: Within this framework, secreted molecules like ligands and extracellular inhibitors are represented by diffusible nodes, and cell-autonomous components such as receptors and kinases are represented by non-diffusible nodes.
evidence: This describes the modeling framework used in the software.

claim: Cell-autonomous components such as receptors and kinases are represented by non-diffusible nodes in RDNets.
source: Within this framework, secreted molecules like ligands and extracellular inhibitors are represented by diffusible nodes, and cell-autonomous components such as receptors and kinases are represented by non-diffusible nodes.
evidence: This describes the modeling framework used in the software.

claim: The software analyzes networks with k interactions between the nodes represented by first order kinetics rates.
source: Our software analyzes networks with k interactions between the nodes; these interactions are represented by first order kinetics rates, where a positive rate corresponds to an activation and a negative rate to an inhibition.
evidence: This describes the mathematical representation used in the software.

claim: A positive rate corresponds to an activation in the network representation.
source: Our software analyzes networks with k interactions between the nodes; these interactions are represented by first order kinetics rates, where a positive rate corresponds to an activation and a negative rate to an inhibition.
evidence: This describes the convention used in the network representation.

claim: A negative rate corresponds to an inhibition in the network representation.
source: Our software analyzes networks with k interactions between the nodes; these interactions are represented by first order kinetics rates, where a positive rate corresponds to an activation and a negative rate to an inhibition.
evidence: This describes the convention used in the network representation.

claim: Type II and Type III networks are more robust to parameter changes than Type I networks.
source: Type II and Type III networks are more robust to parameter changes than Type I networks.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1b with robustness calculations.

claim: Minimal three-node systems can form in-phase and out-of-phase periodic patterns depending on the network topology.
source: Simulations of the possible topologies associated with a given network show that the minimal three-node systems can form in-phase and out-of-phase periodic patterns depending on the network topology.
evidence: This is shown through simulations in Figure 1c.

claim: From an initial 84 possible 3-node networks, 21 reaction-diffusion networks were identified that can form a pattern.
source: Table 1 shows the number of networks identified at each step of our automated mathematical analysis
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 which tracks the filtering process through the analysis steps.

claim: From an initial 11440 possible 4-node networks, 64 reaction-diffusion networks were identified that can form a pattern.
source: Table 1 shows the number of networks identified at each step of our automated mathematical analysis
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 which tracks the filtering process through the analysis steps.

claim: Type III networks have never been characterized before.
source: Type III networks have never been characterized before and surprisingly have patterning conditions that are independent of specific diffusion rates.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the Type III network discovery.

claim: Type III networks have patterning conditions that are independent of specific diffusion rates.
source: Type III networks have never been characterized before and surprisingly have patterning conditions that are independent of specific diffusion rates.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Type III networks are extremely robust to changes in parameter values compared to Type I and Type II networks.
source: We found that Type III networks are not only numerous but also extremely robust to changes in parameter values compared to Type I and Type II networks (Figure 1b, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown through robustness calculations presented in Figure 1b.

claim: A network can form all possible combinations of in-phase or out-of-phase periodic patterns depending on the network topology.
source: Using numerical simulations, we systematically confirmed our mathematical analysis and determined that a network can form all possible combinations of in-phase or out-of-phase periodic patterns depending on the network topology (Figure 1c, Appendix 1).
evidence: This is confirmed through numerical simulations shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Realistic reaction-diffusion networks are intrinsically robust.
source: Together, our results show that realistic reaction-diffusion networks are intrinsically robust, do not require differential diffusivity, and have patterning capabilities identical to classical two-node reaction-diffusion models.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the robustness analysis and network catalog.

claim: Realistic reaction-diffusion networks do not require differential diffusivity.
source: Together, our results show that realistic reaction-diffusion networks are intrinsically robust, do not require differential diffusivity, and have patterning capabilities identical to classical two-node reaction-diffusion models.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that 70% of networks are Type II or Type III.

claim: Realistic reaction-diffusion networks have patterning capabilities identical to classical two-node reaction-diffusion models.
source: Together, our results show that realistic reaction-diffusion networks are intrinsically robust, do not require differential diffusivity, and have patterning capabilities identical to classical two-node reaction-diffusion models.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations showing similar pattern formation.

claim: The novel class of Type III networks suggests a new mechanism of pattern formation that is independent of short-range activation and long-range inhibition based on differential diffusivity.
source: Importantly, the novel class of Type III networks that we discovered suggests a new mechanism of pattern formation that is independent of short-range activation and long-range inhibition based on differential diffusivity.
evidence: This is a major conclusion about the implications of Type III networks.

claim: Two-node networks can only simultaneously satisfy the stability and instability conditions when the diffusion ratio d between the inhibitor and the activator is greater than one.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Murray, 2003), our analysis confirmed that two-node networks can only simultaneously satisfy the stability and instability conditions when the diffusion ratio d between the inhibitor and the activator is greater than one (Figure 2, left column).
evidence: This is confirmed through the graph-theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The differential diffusivity requirement arises from the opposite nature of the stability and instability conditions.
source: Our analysis instead suggests that the differential diffusivity requirement arises from the opposite nature of the stability and instability conditions, which require that the destabilizing feedback must be both higher and lower than the stabilizing feedback.
evidence: This is an insight from the graph-theoretical analysis of pattern-forming conditions.

claim: The diffusion term acts as a unique pivot that can satisfy both stability and instability conditions simultaneously when d > 1 in two-node networks.
source: Since the diffusion term only appears in the destabilizing condition, it assumes the role of a unique pivot that can satisfy both conditions simultaneously when d > 1.
evidence: This is an explanation derived from the mathematical analysis of two-node networks.

claim: The presence of non-diffusible nodes allows feedbacks that do not appear in the instability conditions to act as an additional pivot to satisfy both conditions simultaneously by increasing stability.
source: Our results indicate that the presence of non-diffusible nodes allows feedbacks that do not appear in the instability conditions to act as an additional pivot to satisfy both conditions simultaneously by increasing stability.
evidence: This is an insight from the graph-theoretical analysis explaining Type II networks.

claim: Most Type II networks contain additional negative feedbacks that allow for equal diffusivities.
source: This is the case for most Type II networks (Figure 2, middle column) that contain additional negative feedbacks that allow for equal diffusivities (Klika et al., 2012; Korvasova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Non-diffusible nodes can implement positive feedbacks that can drive the network unstable independently of stabilizing feedbacks and for any diffusion ratio d.
source: Importantly, our analysis also reveals that non-diffusible nodes can implement positive feedbacks that can drive the network unstable independently of stabilizing feedbacks and for any diffusion ratio d.
evidence: This is an insight from the analysis explaining Type III networks.

claim: In Type III networks, the stability and instability conditions are uncoupled and can be simultaneously satisfied for large parameter sets.
source: This is the case for Type III networks (Figure 2, right column), where the stability and instability conditions are uncoupled and can be simultaneously satisfied for large parameter sets.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and explained through the mathematical analysis.

claim: Immobile factors can act as 'capacitors' that retain and amplify perturbations independently of the reactants' diffusion coefficients.
source: This is possible because immobile factors can act as 'capacitors' that retain and amplify perturbations independently of the reactants' diffusion coefficients (see Appendix 3 for details).
evidence: This is an explanation for the mechanism of Type III networks with reference to Appendix 3.

claim: Type III systems represent a fundamentally new pattern formation mechanism that has not been described previously.
source: Such systems represent a fundamentally new pattern formation mechanism that has not been described previously.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of Type III networks.

claim: Models based on 'short-range auto-activation and long-range inhibition' implemented by differential diffusivity are only a special case of a general trade-off between stabilizing and destabilizing feedbacks required for pattern formation.
source: Together, our results show that models based on 'short-range auto-activation and long-range inhibition' implemented by differential diffusivity are only a special case of a general trade-off between stabilizing and destabilizing feedbacks required for pattern formation.
evidence: This is a major theoretical conclusion from the graph-theoretical analysis.

claim: The final aspect of the periodic patterns does not reflect a difference in the range of activators and inhibitors but only a difference in their amplitude.
source: The virtually indistinguishable simulations of Type I networks with differential diffusivity and Type II networks with equal diffusivities reveal that the final aspect of the periodic patterns does not reflect a difference in the range of activators and inhibitors but only a difference in their amplitude (Figure 2c, see Appendix 3 for details).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2c.

claim: In some Type II and Type III networks the relationship between the amplitude of activators and inhibitors can be inverted, such that the perceived range of the activator appears larger than the perceived range of the inhibitor.
source: Indeed, in other Type II and Type III networks the relationship between the amplitude of activators and inhibitors can even be inverted, such that the perceived range of the activator appears larger than the perceived range of the inhibitor.
evidence: This is an observation from simulations of different network types.

claim: Long-range lateral inhibition is not required to limit the expansion of the activator.
source: Therefore, in contrast to previous studies (Kondo and Miura, 2010), we propose that long-range lateral inhibition is not required to limit the expansion of the activator (Appendix 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion that challenges previous understanding, supported by the analysis in Appendix 3.

claim: It has been proposed that Nodal and Lefty implement an activator-inhibitor system that patterns the germ layers and the left-right axis in vertebrates.
source: It has been proposed that Nodal and Lefty implement an activator-inhibitor system that patterns the germ layers and the left-right axis in vertebrates (Chen and Schier, 2001; Shiratori and Hamada, 2006; Shen, 2007; Meinhardt, 2009; Schier, 2009; Kondo and Miura, 2010; Rogers and Schier, 2011; Korvasova et al., 2015) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work on the Nodal/Lefty system.

claim: The self-enhancing activator Nodal has been shown to diffuse 7.5 times slower than the feedback-induced inhibitor Lefty in living zebrafish embryos.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, the self-enhancing activator Nodal has been shown to diffuse 7.5 times slower than the feedback-induced inhibitor Lefty in living zebrafish embryos (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement cited from Müller et al., 2012.

claim: The Nodal/Lefty system has been modeled as a two-component activator-inhibitor system.
source: The Nodal/Lefty system has been modeled as a two-component activator-inhibitor system (Nakamura et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2012), but the influence of cell-autonomous factors including receptors and the well-characterized intracellular signal transduction cascade via phosphorylated Smad2/3 (Schier, 2009) has not been studied.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: The influence of cell-autonomous factors including receptors and the intracellular signal transduction cascade via phosphorylated Smad2/3 on the Nodal/Lefty system has not been studied.
source: The Nodal/Lefty system has been modeled as a two-component activator-inhibitor system (Nakamura et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2012), but the influence of cell-autonomous factors including receptors and the well-characterized intracellular signal transduction cascade via phosphorylated Smad2/3 (Schier, 2009) has not been studied.
evidence: This identifies a gap in previous modeling of the Nodal/Lefty system.

claim: RDNets identified just two possible minimal networks for the Nodal/Lefty system with the specified constraints.
source: With these constraints, our mathematical analysis identified just two possible minimal networks: In one network Lefty inhibits Nodal signaling indirectly at the receptor level, and in the other network Lefty inhibits Nodal directly (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a result from the constrained analysis using RDNets.

claim: In one possible Nodal/Lefty network, Lefty inhibits Nodal signaling indirectly at the receptor level.
source: With these constraints, our mathematical analysis identified just two possible minimal networks: In one network Lefty inhibits Nodal signaling indirectly at the receptor level, and in the other network Lefty inhibits Nodal directly (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is one of the two network topologies identified by RDNets.

claim: In another possible Nodal/Lefty network, Lefty inhibits Nodal directly.
source: With these constraints, our mathematical analysis identified just two possible minimal networks: In one network Lefty inhibits Nodal signaling indirectly at the receptor level, and in the other network Lefty inhibits Nodal directly (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is one of the two network topologies identified by RDNets.

claim: The two predicted mechanisms are in agreement with the two possible mechanisms by which Lefty has been proposed to inhibit Nodal activity.
source: These predictions are in agreement with the two possible mechanisms by which Lefty has been proposed to inhibit Nodal activity: by binding to the Nodal receptor or by directly sequestering Nodal (Chen and Shen, 2004).
evidence: This connects the RDNets predictions to previous experimental proposals.

claim: The role and significance of the two alternative Lefty inhibition mechanisms for Nodal/Lefty-mediated patterning has remained unclear.
source: However, the role and significance of these two alternative mechanisms for Nodal/Lefty-mediated patterning has remained unclear (Cheng et al., 2004; Middleton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating uncertainty in the field.

claim: The first Nodal/Lefty mechanism (Lefty blocks the receptor complex) determines a Type II network.
source: Our mathematical analysis predicts that the first mechanism (Lefty blocks the receptor complex) determines a Type II network, whereas the second mechanism (Lefty blocks Nodal directly) determines a Type III network.
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical analysis of the two network topologies.

claim: The second Nodal/Lefty mechanism (Lefty blocks Nodal directly) determines a Type III network.
source: Our mathematical analysis predicts that the first mechanism (Lefty blocks the receptor complex) determines a Type II network, whereas the second mechanism (Lefty blocks Nodal directly) determines a Type III network.
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical analysis of the two network topologies.

claim: Both Nodal/Lefty models suggest that the system may form patterns without differential diffusivity of activator and inhibitor.
source: Importantly, both models suggest that the Nodal/Lefty system may form patterns without differential diffusivity of activator and inhibitor.
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical analysis of both network types.

claim: The mathematical analysis predicts a possible minimum diffusion ratio d = 0.55 for the Type II Nodal/Lefty network.
source: Using the clearance rate constants of Nodal and Lefty as quantitative constraints, our mathematical analysis predicts a possible minimum diffusion ratio d = 0.55 for the Type II network, whereas the Type III network allows for any combination of diffusion coefficients (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a quantitative prediction from the constrained mathematical analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The Type III Nodal/Lefty network allows for any combination of diffusion coefficients.
source: Using the clearance rate constants of Nodal and Lefty as quantitative constraints, our mathematical analysis predicts a possible minimum diffusion ratio d = 0.55 for the Type II network, whereas the Type III network allows for any combination of diffusion coefficients (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: For unconstrained values of d, the Type III Nodal/Lefty network is more robust to parameter changes than the Type II network.
source: The robustness analysis of the networks shows that for unconstrained valued of d, the Type III network is more robust to parameter changes (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is shown through robustness calculations in Figure 3c.

claim: When the diffusion ratio is fixed to the experimentally quantified value (d = 7.5), the Type II Nodal/Lefty network becomes more robust than the Type III network.
source: However, when we fix the diffusion ratio to the experimentally quantified value (Müller et al., 2012) (d = 7.5), the Type II network becomes more robust than the Type III network (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is shown through robustness calculations in Figure 3d with the experimental constraint.

claim: While Nodal and Lefty do not necessarily need to have different diffusivities to form a pattern, the combination of differential diffusivity and clearance rate constants increases the robustness of the Type II system.
source: This shows that, while Nodal and Lefty do not necessarily need to have different diffusivities to form a pattern, the combination of differential diffusivity and clearance rate constants increases the robustness of the Type II system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the robustness analysis with experimental constraints.

claim: A three-node reaction-diffusion network with two diffusible nodes for BMP and Wnt and a non-diffusible node for Sox9 has previously been derived based on known regulatory interactions.
source: A three-node reaction-diffusion network with two diffusible nodes for the secreted signals BMP and Wnt and a non-diffusible node for the transcription factor Sox9 has previously been derived based on the known regulatory interactions (Figure 4b).
evidence: This references previous work on the BSW digit patterning model.

claim: The three-node BSW network recapitulates the out-of-phase pattern between BMP/Wnt and Sox9 and forms a pattern with extremely low differential diffusivity requirements (d = 1.25).
source: It was shown that this network recapitulates the out-of-phase pattern between BMP/Wnt and Sox9 and forms a pattern with extremely low differential diffusivity requirements (d = 1.25).
evidence: This references previous findings about the BSW network.

claim: The three-node BSW system is a Type II network that can potentially form a pattern even when BMP and Wnt have equal diffusion coefficients.
source: Our comprehensive mathematical analysis reveals that this three-node system is just another topology of the reaction-diffusion network that we analyzed for the extended Nodal/Lefty system; it is therefore a Type II network that can potentially form a pattern even when BMP and Wnt have equal diffusion coefficients.
evidence: This is a new insight from the RDNets analysis of the BSW network.

claim: In previous studies of the BSW network, the possibility of equal diffusivities was missed because the clearance rates of BMP and Wnt had been assumed to be identical.
source: In previous studies, this observation was missed because the clearance rates of BMP and Wnt had been assumed to be identical (Raspopovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This explains why previous studies didn't identify the equal diffusivity possibility.

claim: If BMP is cleared faster than Wnt, the diffusion ratio can be equal to or lower than one (d ≤ 1).
source: However, as we showed in the previous example for Nodal and Lefty, if BMP is cleared faster than Wnt, the diffusion ratio can be equal to or lower than one, d ≤ 1.
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical analysis applied to the BSW system.

claim: The three-node BSW model does not explain the opposite BMP expression and BMP activity patterns observed in the experimental data due to its high abstraction level.
source: The three-node BSW model recapitulates the out-of-phase pattern between BMP/Wnt and Sox9, but due to its high abstraction level it does not explain the opposite BMP expression and BMP activity patterns observed in the experimental data (Figure 4a).
evidence: This identifies a limitation of the previous three-node model.

claim: RDNets predicts that if β-catenin would directly inhibit Sox9, no network could recapitulate the out-of-phase patterns between BMP expression and BMP signaling.
source: Unexpectedly, the screen revealed that if β-catenin would directly inhibit Sox9, no network could recapitulate the out-of-phase patterns between BMP expression and BMP signaling.
evidence: This is a prediction from the constrained RDNets analysis of the five-node BSW network.

claim: The opposite BMP expression and signaling patterns can be obtained when β-catenin indirectly inhibits Sox9 through pSmad1/5/8.
source: By performing a more general screen that left this interaction unconstrained, we found that the opposite BMP expression and signaling patterns can be obtained when β-catenin indirectly inhibits Sox9 through pSmad/1/5/8.
evidence: This is a prediction from the RDNets analysis of the five-node BSW network.

claim: RDNets predicts that the most robust BSW networks include a negative feedback from Sox9 to Wnt.
source: RDNets also predicts that the most robust networks include the following additional interactions: i) a negative feedback from Sox9 to Wnt, ii) a negative feedback from pSmad1/5/8 to BMP, and iii) either a positive feedback from β-catenin to Sox9 or a negative feedback from β-catenin on Wnt (Figure 4b, gray arrows).
evidence: This is a prediction from the RDNets analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: RDNets predicts that the most robust BSW networks include a negative feedback from pSmad1/5/8 to BMP.
source: RDNets also predicts that the most robust networks include the following additional interactions: i) a negative feedback from Sox9 to Wnt, ii) a negative feedback from pSmad1/5/8 to BMP, and iii) either a positive feedback from β-catenin to Sox9 or a negative feedback from β-catenin on Wnt (Figure 4b, gray arrows).
evidence: This is a prediction from the RDNets analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: RDNets predicts that the most robust BSW networks include either a positive feedback from β-catenin to Sox9 or a negative feedback from β-catenin on Wnt.
source: RDNets also predicts that the most robust networks include the following additional interactions: i) a negative feedback from Sox9 to Wnt, ii) a negative feedback from pSmad1/5/8 to BMP, and iii) either a positive feedback from β-catenin to Sox9 or a negative feedback from β-catenin on Wnt (Figure 4b, gray arrows).
evidence: This is a prediction from the RDNets analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The majority of BSW networks identified by the screen was of Type III.
source: Interestingly, the majority of networks identified by our screen was of Type III, suggesting that the proportion of Type III networks increases when more non-diffusible nodes are added.
evidence: This is an observation from the RDNets analysis of the five-node BSW network.

claim: The proportion of Type III networks increases when more non-diffusible nodes are added.
source: Interestingly, the majority of networks identified by our screen was of Type III, suggesting that the proportion of Type III networks increases when more non-diffusible nodes are added.
evidence: This is a general inference from comparing the 3-node and 5-node network analyses.

claim: Reaction-diffusion mechanisms have unique self-organizing capabilities making them appealing for synthetic engineering.
source: Although reaction-diffusion mechanisms have a simple network design, they exhibit unique self-organizing capabilities making them appealing for synthetic engineering (Diambra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation and describes the motivation for synthetic applications.

claim: The synthetic implementation of reaction-diffusion systems has been impeded by the small pattern-forming parameter space of simple two-node models.
source: So far, the synthetic implementation of reaction-diffusion systems has been impeded by the small pattern-forming parameter space of simple two-node models, their requirement for differential diffusivity (Carvalho et al., 2014), and a general gap between abstract models and real sender-receiver reaction-diffusion circuits (Marcon and Sharpe, 2012; Barcena Menendez et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes challenges in synthetic biology supported by citations.

claim: The synthetic implementation of reaction-diffusion systems has been impeded by their requirement for differential diffusivity.
source: So far, the synthetic implementation of reaction-diffusion systems has been impeded by the small pattern-forming parameter space of simple two-node models, their requirement for differential diffusivity (Carvalho et al., 2014), and a general gap between abstract models and real sender-receiver reaction-diffusion circuits (Marcon and Sharpe, 2012; Barcena Menendez et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes challenges in synthetic biology supported by citations.

claim: There is a general gap between abstract models and real sender-receiver reaction-diffusion circuits.
source: So far, the synthetic implementation of reaction-diffusion systems has been impeded by the small pattern-forming parameter space of simple two-node models, their requirement for differential diffusivity (Carvalho et al., 2014), and a general gap between abstract models and real sender-receiver reaction-diffusion circuits (Marcon and Sharpe, 2012; Barcena Menendez et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes challenges in synthetic biology supported by citations.

claim: RDNets provides a comprehensive catalog of reaction-diffusion networks that do not require differential diffusivity of the signaling molecules.
source: RDNets provides a comprehensive catalog of reaction-diffusion networks that do not require differential diffusivity of the signaling molecules, which enables bioengineers to explore new mechanisms to form periodic spatial patterns in a robust manner.
evidence: This describes the utility of RDNets for synthetic biology applications.

claim: An existing synthetic circuit for cell-cell communication in yeast introduced a diffusible plant hormone, cytokinin isopentenyladenine (IP), and its receptor AtCRE1 into yeast.
source: The original synthetic circuit introduced a diffusible plant hormone, cytokinin isopentenyladenine (IP), and its receptor AtCRE1 into yeast (Figure 5a).
evidence: This references the Chen and Weiss 2005 synthetic circuit.

claim: The Chen and Weiss synthetic circuit was used to implement a sender-receiver and a quorum sensing mechanism based on a positive feedback loop between IP-signaling and IP.
source: This circuit was used to implement a sender-receiver and a quorum sensing mechanism based on a positive feedback loop between IP-signaling and IP (Figure 5a).
evidence: This describes the functionality of the Chen and Weiss 2005 circuit.

claim: At least two diffusible nodes are required to form a pattern in reaction-diffusion systems.
source: Since at least two diffusible nodes are required to form a pattern (Murray, 2003), we screened minimal 4-node networks that include the engineered positive feedback and candidate interactions with another diffusible node.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of reaction-diffusion systems supported by citation.

claim: The high-throughput analysis identified 16 minimal reaction-diffusion networks for the synthetic circuit extension (5 Type I, 3 Type II, 8 Type III).
source: With these constraints, our high-throughput analysis identified 16 minimal reaction-diffusion networks (5 Type I, 3 Type II, 8 Type III), of which the Type II and Type III networks were most robust to parameter changes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the RDNets analysis for synthetic circuit design.

claim: The Type II and Type III synthetic networks were most robust to parameter changes.
source: With these constraints, our high-throughput analysis identified 16 minimal reaction-diffusion networks (5 Type I, 3 Type II, 8 Type III), of which the Type II and Type III networks were most robust to parameter changes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A simple extension to the Chen and Weiss circuit could be obtained by destabilizing the signaling hormone and the receptor to increase their turn-over.
source: This network suggests that a simple extension to the circuit developed in Chen and Weiss (2005) could be obtained by a) destabilizing the signaling hormone and the receptor to increase their turn-over (c1, c2), and b) introducing another hormone that signals through the same receptor and implements a negative feedback loop to its own expression or activity (c3, Figure 5a - right).
evidence: This is a design suggestion based on the RDNets analysis.

claim: A simple extension to the Chen and Weiss circuit could be obtained by introducing another hormone that signals through the same receptor and implements a negative feedback loop to its own expression or activity.
source: This network suggests that a simple extension to the circuit developed in Chen and Weiss (2005) could be obtained by a) destabilizing the signaling hormone and the receptor to increase their turn-over (c1, c2), and b) introducing another hormone that signals through the same receptor and implements a negative feedback loop to its own expression or activity (c3, Figure 5a - right).
evidence: This is a design suggestion based on the RDNets analysis.

claim: RDNets provides the mathematical formulae of pattern forming conditions in addition to revealing possible topologies.
source: In addition to revealing possible topologies, our automated analysis provides the mathematical formulae of pattern forming conditions.
evidence: This describes a feature of the RDNets software output.

claim: The newly introduced negative feedback in the synthetic circuit has to be stronger than the positive feedback and decay rates.
source: With these constraints, RDNets determined that the newly introduced negative feedback has to be stronger than the positive feedback and decay rates (Figure 5c - right).
evidence: This is a quantitative prediction from the constrained RDNets analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Other Type III synthetic networks are even more robust to parameter changes than the Type II network presented, but they appear to require the design of more complex synthetic circuits.
source: This specific synthetic network represents only one possibility. We find other Type III networks to be even more robust to parameter changes, but they appear to require the design of more complex synthetic circuits (Appendix 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the catalog of synthetic networks with reference to Appendix 4.

claim: RDNets can be used to automatically derive kinetic models that can simulate the reaction-diffusion network.
source: Once a synthetic network is designed, RDNets can also be used to automatically derive kinetic models that can simulate the reaction-diffusion network (Figure 5d,e, Appendix 5).
evidence: This describes a feature of the RDNets software with reference to simulations in Figure 5d,e.

claim: Numerical simulations can be used to investigate the qualitative aspect of the pattern and its spatial periodicity.
source: Numerical simulations can be used to investigate the qualitative aspect of the pattern and its spatial periodicity.
evidence: This describes the utility of simulations for pattern analysis.

claim: RDNets can be run from most web browsers and does not demand large computational power.
source: First, RDNets can be run from most web browsers and does not demand large computational power.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the RDNets software.

claim: The mathematical analysis of RDNets yields closed-form solutions and is complete, in contrast to numerical simulations that can necessarily only sample from a small region of the entire parameter space.
source: Second, our mathematical analysis yields closed-form solutions and is complete, in contrast to numerical simulations that can necessarily only sample from a small region of the entire parameter space.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the analytical approach over numerical methods.

claim: RDNets derives the conditions for pattern formation and therefore provides mechanistic explanatory power to the users.
source: Third, RDNets derives the conditions for pattern formation and therefore provides mechanistic explanatory power to the users.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the RDNets approach.

claim: RDNets helps to identify reaction-diffusion topologies that are in agreement with qualitative and quantitative experimental constraints.
source: In addition, it helps to identify reaction-diffusion topologies that are in agreement with qualitative and quantitative experimental constraints, which makes it an unprecedented tool for users that aim to study developmental patterning networks or to design reaction-diffusion synthetic circuits.
evidence: This describes the utility of RDNets for experimental biologists.

claim: The analytical approach of RDNets is both comprehensive and informative.
source: Motivated by theoretical studies that showed that non-diffusible factors can influence pattern forming conditions, we used our software to systematically explore the effect of non-diffusible reactants in reaction-diffusion models. Our analytical approach is both comprehensive and informative and reveals that depending on the network topology, reaction-diffusion systems can belong to three classes: Type I systems that require differential diffusivity, Type II systems that can form patterns with equal diffusivity, and Type III systems that form patterns independent of specific diffusion rates.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the advantages of the approach.

claim: The novel class of Type III networks challenges models of short-range activation and long-range inhibition based on differential diffusivity that have dominated the field of developmental and theoretical biology for decades.
source: In particular, the novel class of Type III networks has not been described before and challenges models of short-range activation and long-range inhibition based on differential diffusivity that have dominated the field of developmental and theoretical biology for decades (see Appendix 3 for details).
evidence: This is a major conclusion about the implications of Type III networks for the field.

claim: The high general robustness of the Type III Nodal/Lefty network might have played a role for the evolution of the Nodal/Lefty reaction-diffusion system in the first place.
source: We propose that the high general robustness of the Type III network might have played a role for the evolution of the Nodal/Lefty reaction-diffusion system in the first place, and that the indirect Nodal signaling inhibition of Type II networks might have been fine-tuned during evolution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis based on the robustness analysis.

claim: The indirect Nodal signaling inhibition of Type II networks might have been fine-tuned during evolution.
source: We propose that the high general robustness of the Type III network might have played a role for the evolution of the Nodal/Lefty reaction-diffusion system in the first place, and that the indirect Nodal signaling inhibition of Type II networks might have been fine-tuned during evolution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis based on the robustness analysis.

claim: The five-node BSW model accurately reflects the previously puzzling opposite pattern of BMP ligands and BMP signaling.
source: Our analysis identified realistic network topologies that accurately reflect the previously puzzling opposite pattern of BMP ligands and BMP signaling and predicts novel interactions between network components.
evidence: This is a result from the RDNets analysis of the five-node BSW network.

claim: The five-node BSW model predicts novel interactions between network components.
source: Our analysis identified realistic network topologies that accurately reflect the previously puzzling opposite pattern of BMP ligands and BMP signaling and predicts novel interactions between network components.
evidence: This is a result from the RDNets analysis of the five-node BSW network.

claim: Identifying a comprehensive catalog of gene networks that can perform a certain behavior has been shown to be a successful strategy to uncover the design space of stripe-forming networks.
source: Identifying a comprehensive catalog of gene networks that can perform a certain behavior has been shown to be a successful strategy to uncover the design space of stripe-forming networks (Cotterell and Sharpe, 2010), which can be directly useful to synthetic biology.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on stripe-forming networks.

claim: A whole family of stripe-forming network mechanisms have been synthetically constructed in bacteria.
source: In particular, this approach permitted a whole family of network mechanisms to be synthetically constructed in bacteria – all capable of forming a gene expression stripe in a bacterial lawn (Schaerli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Schaerli et al. 2014 study.

claim: RDNets networks explicitly include non-diffusible factors that mediate signaling and are easy to relate with sender-receiver synthetic toolkits.
source: These networks explicitly include non-diffusible factors that mediate signaling and are easy to relate with sender-receiver synthetic toolkits (Barcena Menendez et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes an advantage of the RDNets networks for synthetic biology.

claim: The majority of realistic reaction-diffusion networks eliminate the differential diffusivity requirement that is difficult to implement synthetically.
source: In addition, we found that the majority of realistic reaction-diffusion networks eliminate the differential diffusivity requirement that is difficult to implement synthetically (Carvalho et al., 2014; Barcena Menendez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the finding that 70% of networks are Type II or Type III, with citations to synthetic biology challenges.

claim: The possibility to use qualitative and quantitative constraints to screen for reaction-diffusion networks makes RDNets a unique tool to customize patterning systems from initial starting networks.
source: The possibility to use qualitative and quantitative constraints to screen for reaction-diffusion networks makes RDNets a unique tool to customize patterning systems from initial starting networks.
evidence: This describes a unique capability of the RDNets software.

claim: The pattern-forming conditions derived by RDNets can be used to estimate parameter ranges and network robustness.
source: Moreover, the pattern-forming conditions derived by the software can be used to estimate parameter ranges and network robustness.
evidence: This describes a utility of the RDNets output.

claim: Each network is associated with a set of topologies that exhaustively determine all the in-phase and out-of-phase relations between periodic patterns.
source: Particularly promising is our finding that each network is associated with a set of topologies that exhaustively determine all the in-phase and out-of-phase relations between periodic patterns (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5d and describes a feature of the network catalog.

claim: It is possible to design network topologies that promote the co-localized expression of any desired combination of factors.
source: It is therefore possible to design network topologies that promote the co-localized expression of any desired combination of factors.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding about in-phase and out-of-phase patterns.

claim: The co-localized expression of differentiating factors can be used to induce specific tissues in tissue engineering applications.
source: This will enable novel applications in tissue engineering, where the co-localized expression of differentiating factors can be used to induce specific tissues (Kaplan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a potential application supported by citation to tissue engineering work.

claim: Reaction-diffusion mechanisms have three-dimensional pattern-forming capabilities.
source: Coupled with the three-dimensional pattern-forming capabilities of reaction-diffusion mechanisms (Figure 5e), this could be used to devise new strategies for engineering scaffolds or tissues with complex architecture.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the 3D simulation shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The analysis defines new concepts of reaction-diffusion-mediated patterning that are directly relevant for developmental and synthetic biology.
source: In summary, our analysis defines new concepts of reaction-diffusion-mediated patterning that are directly relevant for developmental and synthetic biology.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the work.

claim: The RDNets approach can be extended to numerous other patterning processes.
source: We demonstrate three applications of our software RDNets to understand developmental mechanisms and to design synthetic patterning systems, but this approach can be extended to numerous other patterning processes (Economou et al., 2012; Menshykau et al., 2012; Hagiwara et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other patterning systems.

claim: RDNets will contribute to the wide-spread use of mathematical biology.
source: We therefore expect that RDNets will contribute to the wide-spread use of mathematical biology and that a similar approach could be applied to other dynamical processes such as oscillations and traveling waves (Bement et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prediction about the impact of the software.

claim: A similar approach to RDNets could be applied to other dynamical processes such as oscillations and traveling waves.
source: We therefore expect that RDNets will contribute to the wide-spread use of mathematical biology and that a similar approach could be applied to other dynamical processes such as oscillations and traveling waves (Bement et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications supported by citation.

claim: RDNets was written in Mathematica.
source: Our web-based software RDNets was written in Mathematica (Wolfram Research Inc., Champaign, Illinois) and is available at http://www.RDNets.com.
evidence: This is a technical detail about the software implementation.

claim: RDNets requires only the installation of the freely available Wolfram CDF player plugin.
source: RDNets requires only the installation of the freely available Wolfram CDF player plugin (http://www.wolfram.com/cdf-player/).
evidence: This is a technical requirement for using the software.

claim: Minimal reaction-diffusion networks are defined as the networks with the minimal number of edges k that can form a reaction-diffusion pattern.
source: Our analysis aims to identify minimal reaction-diffusion networks, defined as the networks with the minimal number of edges k that can form a reaction-diffusion pattern.
evidence: This defines a key concept used in the analysis.

claim: Minimal 2-node reaction-diffusion networks must have 2x2=4 edges.
source: In the case of 2-node networks, it has been described that minimal reaction-diffusion networks must have 2x2=4 edges (Murray, 2003), and therefore only a completely connected network is allowed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Murray 2003.

claim: The completely connected 2-node network allows for only two reaction-diffusion topologies: the 'activator-inhibitor system' that forms in-phase periodic patterns, and the 'substrate-depleted model' that forms out-of-phase periodic patterns.
source: This completely connected 2-node network allows for only two reaction-diffusion topologies: the 'activator-inhibitor system' that forms in-phase periodic patterns, and the 'substrate-depleted model' that forms out-of-phase periodic patterns.
evidence: This is established knowledge about 2-node reaction-diffusion systems.

claim: According to the Abel-Ruffini theorem, there is no general algebraic solution for systems with more than four nodes.
source: According to the Abel-Ruffini theorem, there is no general algebraic solution for systems with more than four nodes.
evidence: This is a mathematical theorem that limits the analytical approach.

claim: In practice many five-node networks can be solved if the constraints specified in the input of RDNets lead to a simplification of the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial.
source: However, in practice many five-node networks can be solved if the constraints specified in the input of RDNets lead to a simplification of the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial, as is the case for the five-node digit patterning network (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated with the five-node BSW network analysis.
